name: Hexylresorcinol

card.summary: A skincare and antiseptic ingredient (4-hexylresorcinol) used in anti-aging and brightening creams to even skin tone.

quick.overview:
4-Hexylresorcinol is an organic compound with local anaesthetic, antiseptic and anthelmintic properties. It appears in throat lozenges, antiseptic solutions and in cosmetic anti-aging creams.
In skincare it is promoted for evening skin tone and fine lines. Johnson & Johnson uses it in Neutrogena, Aveeno and RoC products, and other brands include Murad and Clarins [1]. Published research is mostly on wound healing and bone work, not facial skin [2][3].
quick.how: It is found as an ingredient in leave-on creams and serums used with the rest of a skincare routine, typically applied to the face.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes a 2009 study found some estrogen-like activity as a food additive, while a 2020 study found no change in estrogen receptor expression in cells [1]. Irritation is possible as with any topical active.

lead: 4-Hexylresorcinol (E586) is an organic compound with local anaesthetic, antiseptic and anthelmintic properties. It is used in throat lozenges and antiseptics and was sold as an anthelmintic called Crystoids [1].

In cosmetics, it is used as an anti-aging ingredient by companies including Johnson & Johnson (Neutrogena, Aveeno, RoC), Mary Kay, Clarins, Unilever, Murad and Arbonne [1]. Sytheon markets it as Synovea HR [1].
Laboratory and surgical reviews describe it as an inducer of M2 macrophages and a pharmacologic chaperone that reduces NF-kB signalling and increases angiogenesis and bone formation in wounds [2][3].

angle.text: Brands include it in anti-aging and brightening formulas aimed at skin tone and fine lines. Published research on it concerns wound healing and bone work rather than facial pigmentation.

paras: Used in anti-aging creams by several major brands [1].
Throat lozenges, topical antiseptic for small skin infections, and an older anthelmintic use [1].

Reviews report it induces endoplasmic reticulum stress and changes protein folding, inhibits NF-kB and TNF-alpha, and increases VEGF and TGF-beta1, which promotes angiogenesis and bone formation [3]. It has been used in bone grafts and dental implant coatings [2].

A 2009 study reported estrogenic activity as a food additive; a 2020 study found no change in estrogen receptors in MCF-7 cells [1]. A 1989 toxicology commentary discussed apparent antitumorigenic findings in a bioassay [4].
No studies on facial brightening have been found. Surgical and wound-healing research is described in reviews [2][3].
